prompt: Does the bucket have to be public for CloudFront to serve our recordings?
ten_second: No. The bucket stays private and trusts only your CloudFront distribution. A signed link with an end time decides who can play a recording.
sixty_second: The short answer is no. The bucket stays private.
It works like this. The bucket is where your recordings are stored.
The distribution is your CloudFront setup in front of the bucket.
CloudFront sends authenticated requests to the bucket.
The bucket policy allows CloudFront, and only for requests from your distribution.
So a direct link to the bucket fails. Every viewer goes through CloudFront.
And the transfer from the bucket to CloudFront is free.
The thing to watch is this: a private bucket doesn't decide which users can play.
For that, the app gives each signed-in user a signed link with an end time.
After that time, the link stops working.
In your case, a playback link works for a few minutes today.
Should it work longer for very long calls?

key_points.point: With origin access control, the bucket policy allows the CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com) only when the request is on behalf of your distribution.
accept: the bucket trusts only our distribution
the bucket policy allows CloudFront for our distribution

key_points.point: Users reach the files through the distribution and cannot access them directly by using Amazon S3 URLs, so no one bypasses CloudFront.
accept: a direct S3 link fails
nobody can go around CloudFront

key_points.point: AWS recommends origin access control (OAC) instead of the older origin access identity (OAI).
accept: use origin access control
OAC is the recommended way

key_points.point: A CloudFront signed URL has an ending date and time, after which the URL is no longer valid.
accept: the signed link expires
the link stops working after a set time

key_points.point: Data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, and edge locations closer to users give lower latency.
accept: the bucket to CloudFront transfer costs nothing
users abroad get faster playback

key_points.point: AWS recommends trusted key groups as the signer for signed URLs and signed cookies.
accept: sign with a trusted key group

must_not_say.error: we make the bucket public but use random file names
must_not_say.correct: AWS recommends CloudFront in front of the bucket so that it's not publicly accessible. Origin access control keeps the bucket private.

must_not_say.error: an origin access identity is the recommended way to keep the bucket private
must_not_say.correct: AWS recommends origin access control. An origin access identity doesn't work for all scenarios, for example dynamic requests to Amazon S3.

follow_ups.question: Can we limit a recording link to the computers of one customer office?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. When you create a signed URL, you can also set the IP address or range of addresses of the computers that can access the content.

follow_ups.question: Does CloudFront also make playback faster for our users abroad?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. CloudFront serves content from edge locations closer to the users, so latency is lower. And data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free.

prompt: CloudFront or Global Accelerator: which one makes our game faster for players around the world?
persona: a game studio founder in office hours
ten_second: Both use AWS edge locations near your players. CloudFront caches downloads such as patches. Global Accelerator carries live TCP or UDP game traffic.
sixty_second: Both services meet your players at AWS edge locations near them. The difference is what they carry.
It works like this. CloudFront works with web content over HTTP.
It keeps copies of files, such as patches and images, at the edge.
When a player asks for a cached file, the edge location returns it.
Global Accelerator works with TCP and UDP traffic.
It proxies the packets at the edge to your load balancers or instances in AWS Regions.
Players connect to static IP addresses, and failover between Regions is fast.
The thing to watch is that many games need both services.
CloudFront for downloads, and Global Accelerator for live play.
In your case, patches are large files that many players download.
Does your live game traffic use UDP, and in which Regions does it run?
skeleton: Global Accelerator: TCP, UDP, static IPs

key_points.point: CloudFront improves performance for both cacheable content (such as images and videos) and dynamic content.
accept: CloudFront caches files at the edge
CloudFront is for web content

key_points.point: Global Accelerator improves TCP or UDP applications by proxying packets at the edge to applications in AWS Regions.
accept: Global Accelerator proxies packets
it carries TCP and UDP traffic to the Regions

key_points.point: Global Accelerator fits non-HTTP use cases such as gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP, and fast regional failover.
accept: Global Accelerator fits UDP games
it gives fast failover between Regions

key_points.point: A new accelerator gets two IPv4 static IP addresses.
accept: players connect to fixed IP addresses
the accelerator has static addresses

key_points.point: CloudFront supports content that can be sent using the HTTP or WebSocket protocols.
accept: CloudFront is for HTTP and WebSocket

key_points.point: When the object is in the cache of the edge location, CloudFront returns it to the user from there.
accept: a cache hit is answered at the edge

must_not_say.error: Global Accelerator caches your game files at the edge
must_not_say.correct: Global Accelerator proxies TCP or UDP packets at the edge to applications in AWS Regions. CloudFront is the service that returns cached copies.

must_not_say.error: CloudFront can carry our live UDP game traffic
must_not_say.correct: CloudFront supports content sent using the HTTP or WebSocket protocols. UDP traffic is a use case for Global Accelerator.

must_not_say.error: Global Accelerator replaces your load balancers
must_not_say.correct: Global Accelerator sends traffic to endpoints such as Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers or EC2 instances. The load balancers stay.

follow_ups.question: Can our partners allow-list the addresses of the game?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. A new accelerator gets two IPv4 static IP addresses from independent network zones. Partners allow-list those addresses, not your instances.

follow_ups.question: Do both services help against DDoS attacks?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. Both services integrate with AWS Shield for DDoS protection.

prompt: Every release changes our JavaScript files. Do we invalidate the whole cache each time, or is there a better way?
ten_second: Put a version in your file names. A new name is a new file everywhere. Keep invalidation for surprises.
sixty_second: The short answer is: put a version in your file names.
Keep invalidation for the unexpected cases.
It works like this. A new file name is a new object for CloudFront.
It's also new for browsers and company proxies, so they don't return the old copy.
Your HTML page points to the new names after each release.
AWS still recommends an expiration date on the files, even with versions.
The thing to watch is the real reason. It isn't mainly cost.
A wildcard path counts as one path, even when it removes many files.
The problem is that invalidation can't reach copies in browsers and proxies.
Users can keep seeing the old version until those copies expire.
In your case, look at your build tool.
Does it already add a hash to your file names?

key_points.point: For frequent updates, AWS recommends that you primarily use file versioning, not invalidation.
accept: version the file names
use versioned names instead of invalidation

key_points.point: Versioning controls which file a request returns, even when the user has a copy cached locally or behind a corporate caching proxy.
accept: browsers and proxies get the new file
invalidation does not reach browser copies

key_points.point: AWS says to use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances.
accept: invalidation is for surprises
invalidate only when something goes wrong

key_points.point: Even if you version your files, AWS still recommends that you set an expiration date.
accept: still set an expiry
keep a cache lifetime on versioned files

key_points.point: A path with the * wildcard counts as one path, and the first 1,000 invalidation paths each month are free.
accept: a wildcard is one path
invalidation is cheap for a few paths

must_not_say.correct: The first 1,000 invalidation paths that you submit each month are free. You pay for each path after that.

must_not_say.error: turn on S3 Versioning to update the files
must_not_say.correct: AWS recommends a version identifier in file names or in folder names. That is a naming practice, not a bucket setting.

must_not_say.error: set every TTL to zero so users always get new files
must_not_say.correct: If Minimum TTL, Maximum TTL and Default TTL are all set to 0, CloudFront caching is disabled.

follow_ups.question: What if a broken file is already cached and must go now?
follow_ups.answer: That is the unexpected case that invalidation is for. A path with the * wildcard counts as one path, and the first 1,000 invalidation paths each month are free.

follow_ups.question: How long does CloudFront keep a file if our origin sends no cache headers?
follow_ups.answer: Then CloudFront uses the Default TTL of the cache behavior. Its default value is 86400 seconds, which is one day.

prompt: CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge: where should our token check run?
ten_second: If a key in the function can check the token, use CloudFront Functions. If the check must call your user service, use Lambda@Edge.
sixty_second: Both let you run code in CloudFront, close to your users. The difference is what the code can reach.
It works like this. CloudFront Functions are for short, light tasks.
Checking a JSON web token in the request headers is one of them.
They run in under a millisecond, but they have no network access.
Lambda@Edge runs longer, and it can make network calls.
For example, it can call your user service to confirm credentials.
The thing to watch is cost and key data.
CloudFront Functions cost a fraction of the price of Lambda@Edge.
Keep the key data in CloudFront KeyValueStore, so you update it without new code.
In your case, it depends on the token.
Is it a signed JSON web token, or does the check need a database lookup?

key_points.point: CloudFront Functions suit request authorization: they can validate authorization tokens, such as JSON web tokens (JWT), by inspecting authorization headers.
accept: a function can check a JSON web token
token checks fit CloudFront Functions

key_points.point: CloudFront Functions have no network access, no file system access and no access to the request body.
accept: CloudFront Functions cannot call other services
no network calls from CloudFront Functions

key_points.point: A Lambda@Edge function can make network calls to external resources, for example to confirm user credentials.
accept: Lambda@Edge can call our user service
Lambda@Edge has network access

key_points.point: CloudFront Functions run in submillisecond time, and Lambda@Edge functions can run up to 30 seconds.
accept: functions run in under a millisecond
Lambda@Edge runs longer

key_points.point: CloudFront Functions cost a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge.
accept: CloudFront Functions are cheaper

key_points.point: CloudFront KeyValueStore lets a function read key value data that you update independently of the function code.
accept: keep the keys in KeyValueStore

must_not_say.error: CloudFront Functions can call your API to check the token
must_not_say.correct: CloudFront Functions have no network access. A check that calls another service needs Lambda@Edge.
CloudFront Functions is meant to complement Lambda@Edge, not replace it. You can use both on different event triggers within the same cache behavior.
CloudFront Functions run in submillisecond time. Lambda@Edge functions can run up to 30 seconds.

follow_ups.question: Can we use both in the same distribution?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. You can use CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge on different event triggers within the same cache behavior.

follow_ups.question: How big can a CloudFront function be?
follow_ups.answer: The maximum function size is 10 KB, and this quota isn't adjustable. For more data, you create a key value store.
